newsitem.title: CHINA: China officials deny suspension of copper imports.
newsitem.headline: China officials deny suspension of copper imports.

text.p: Chinese officials on Monday dismissed reports that authorities had issued a directive suspending copper imports and ordering traders not to sell their copper to hold up prices.

However, an official of the China National Nonferrous Metals Import and Export Corp said the firm that is responsible for China's trade in copper had last week recommended traders hold their positions to wait for further price rises.
But this week, the firm was urging traders to sell because prices were seen as favourable, he said.
The company held a one-day seminar last Tuesday to discuss the current domestic and international copper market.
"It was just a regular meeting inside the company, no directives were issued," said the official who declined to be further identified.
"We just urged firms holding hedging positions to hold their positions to wait for further price rises," he said. "It is not up to us to decide whether to import, that will be decided by the market."
However, he said this week prices were rising -- just as the company had forecast last week.
Domestic copper prices were expected to rise in the short term and it was now a good time to sell, he said.
"We think firms engaged in hedging should enter the market now and sell," he said. "Copper firms should reduce exports because they will not make good profits."

Imports were expected to increase in the short term because of higher domestic prices, but could fall in the longer term because domestic prices were seen dropping as imports rose, the official added.
"Copper prices could hit 24,000 yuan ($2,891) per tonne and then enter into a relatively long period of technical correction."

Shanghai copper futures opened higher on Monday on reports of a directive to suspend imports and an order not to sell. The most active June 1996 contract opened at 23,800 yuan per tonne and rose further to 24,080 yuan in early trading.
